---
title: "Read a tree-volume regression model"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Read a tree-volume regression model}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

How much does a tree's estimated timber volume change with trunk diameter,
after accounting for height? We will read one regression result and connect
its coefficients, uncertainty and residual error. In this sample, an extra
inch of diameter is associated with about 4.71 extra cubic feet of volume
at a fixed height. The remaining residual scatter is about 3.88 cubic feet.

## Understand the measurements

**Example data: R's built-in trees dataset**

The 31 observations are felled black cherry trees. `Volume` is timber volume
in cubic feet and `Height` is height in feet. Despite its name, `Girth` is
trunk **diameter**, measured in inches at 4 feet 6 inches above the ground.
Reading the data documentation matters: interpreting this column as
circumference would give the slope the wrong physical meaning.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r data, message=FALSE}
library(olsrr)
tree_data <- datasets::trees
stopifnot(nrow(tree_data) == 31L, !anyNA(tree_data))
head(tree_data)
```

Every row has all three measurements, so no tree is dropped. This example
describes associations in the observed trees. It does not establish a
growth law or show what an intervention on height would cause. Keeping the
units beside the data helps distinguish a coefficient from a measure without
units, such as R-squared.

## Fit one model

```{r model}
volume_model <- lm(Volume ~ Girth + Height, data = tree_data)
```

This additive model lets volume change linearly with diameter and height.
Each slope describes a comparison holding the other predictor fixed.
The formula does not encode the geometric relationship between diameter
and volume, which might motivate a curved or transformed model later.
For now the aim is to understand exactly what this fitted summary says.

## Read the regression table

```{r regression}
ols_regress(volume_model)
```

The **Beta** estimate for `Girth`, 4.708, means about 4.71 additional cubic
feet per additional inch of diameter, comparing trees of the same height.
For `Height`, 0.339 means about 0.34 additional cubic feet per extra foot of
height at a fixed diameter. Standardized betas express effects on a
different scale; use the unstandardized Beta column for these statements
in inches, feet and cubic feet.

The **Std. Error** column measures uncertainty in each estimated slope.
The **lower** and **upper** columns give its 95% confidence interval under
the model assumptions: about 4.17 to 5.25 for diameter and 0.073 to 0.606
for height. The height estimate is less precise relative to its size.
These intervals concern conditional mean slopes, not the volumes of
individual trees. The p-values test zero coefficients conditional on the
other term; they do not measure the probability that a predictor matters.

The intercept is about -57.99 cubic feet at zero diameter and zero height.
Neither value describes a tree in this sample. This is a warning against
extrapolation, rather than evidence of negative timber volume.

## Connect the output to base R

```{r base-comparison}
base_summary <- summary(volume_model)
knitr::kable(base_summary$coefficients[, c("Estimate", "Std. Error")],
             digits = 3, caption = "The same coefficients and standard errors from summary(lm(...)).")
```

The estimates and standard errors agree with the parameter table above:
olsrr presents information from the same fitted model. R's residual
standard error, `base_summary$sigma`, is the RMSE reported here. Its value
of 3.882 cubic feet is the square root of residual sum of squares divided
by 28 residual degrees of freedom. It describes remaining scatter, not a
fixed error allowance for each new prediction.

## Understand the ANOVA decomposition

The regression output already includes an ANOVA table. `ols_anova()` lets
you request just that part when the overall fit is your question.

```{r anova, results="hide"}
volume_anova <- ols_anova(volume_model)
volume_anova
```

In that table, the total sum of squares, 8106.084, divides into 7684.163
attributed to the regression and 421.921 left in the residuals. Dividing
7684.163 by 8106.084 gives R-squared, 0.948. This is variation explained
in these trees, not a percentage accuracy guarantee for future volumes.

There are two regression degrees of freedom, one for each slope, and
28 residual degrees of freedom: 31 observations minus three estimated
coefficients, including the intercept. Dividing each sum of squares by
its degrees of freedom gives the mean squares. Their ratio is the overall
F statistic, 254.972. Its null is that both slopes are zero. This joint
test does not identify which model shape is adequate or validate the
error assumptions.

The concrete next task is to inspect residual shape and spread before
relying on the confidence intervals. Continue with
[residual diagnostics](residual-diagnostics.html), or revisit
[getting started](getting-started.html). The help for
[`ols_regress()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_regress.html) and
[`ols_anova()`](https://olsrr.rsquaredacademy.com/reference/ols_anova.html) covers the remaining table fields
and supported interfaces.
